misconceptions.description: Conserving linear momentum during impacts even when impulsive constraint reactions are present
misconceptions.trigger: learner conserves linear momentum across a pinned-rod impact
misconceptions.feedback: Pinned constraints exert impulsive reactions during impact. Linear momentum is NOT conserved. Angular momentum about the pin IS conserved because the reaction has zero moment about itself.

misconceptions.description: Assuming a body's moment of inertia about a fixed axis cannot change
misconceptions.trigger: learner says ω cannot change without external torque
misconceptions.feedback: Configuration change (pulling arms in, deploying solar panels) changes I_G. With angular momentum conserved, ω must adjust to keep I_G ω constant. This is the skater spin-up effect.

misconceptions.description: Using center-of-mass velocity in the coefficient-of-restitution equation for an eccentric impact
misconceptions.trigger: learner writes e = (v_G,B' - v_G,A') / (v_G,A - v_G,B) for rotating bodies
misconceptions.feedback: Restitution operates at the contact point. For rotating bodies the contact-point velocity equals v_G + ω × r_G→contact. Using v_G alone misses the rotational contribution at the contact.

misconceptions.description: Using centroidal moment of inertia I_G when the angular momentum is taken about a fixed point
misconceptions.trigger: learner writes ∫M_O dt = I_G (ω₂ - ω₁) for a pinned body
misconceptions.feedback: Angular momentum about a fixed pin uses I_O = I_G + Md² by the parallel-axis theorem. Using only I_G underestimates the rotational resistance.
